Fair pushback—my first idea leaned into a well-trodden vein of site-specific "ghosts of places past" work, even if the specific execution felt personal to me. Let me pivot to something I've never voiced out loud before, something tiny and messy and deliberately unmarketable.

I'd make one-of-a-kind handbound zines from repurposed vintage paper: 1950s grocery store receipt books, faded library checkout cards, scraped 1970s wallpaper edges, and smudged children's workbook pages with half-erased math problems. Each zine would be a "found artifact" from a fictional alternate micro-town I'm calling Hollowed Grove—a place where people who vanished "quietly" (no police reports, no missing person posters, just everyone forgetting they existed) end up settling.

Each zine would be a jumble of hand-lettered, smudged text and tiny, half-doodled drawings: a grocery list with items like "pickled dandelion wine (glows faintly at midnight)" and "a jar of names no one remembers anymore," a library checkout card for a book titled *The Half-Life of Unspoken Goodbyes* with checkout dates that don't line up with any real calendar, a handwritten apology note that's 70% crossed out, and a child's drawing of a house with no doors, only windows that look into other identical windows.

The interactive twist is a tiny sealed envelope tucked in the back of every zine. Inside is a handwritten prompt asking the reader to do a small, private, unrecorded act: write a secret they've never told anyone and bury it under a tree, leave a half-eaten candy bar on a park bench with a note that says "for the person who feels invisible," record a 10-second voice memo of a song they can't remember the name of and delete it immediately. The envelope also has a PO box address where they can send back a single tiny object that represents their act—no letter, no explanation, just the object. I'd lock every returned object (a crumpled gum wrapper, a pressed clover, a broken bottle cap) in a dented metal box I keep in my closet, never to be exhibited or talked about publicly.

The themes here are the invisible edges of invisibility: choosing to vanish instead of being forced out, the small, uncelebrated acts of vulnerability that no one ever witnesses, and the way we all carry tiny, unshared worlds that feel as real as the one we live in. It's not a grand statement, it's a quiet, private conversation between me and the handful of people who stumble across these zines (I'd leave them in laundromat folding tables, bus stop bench cracks, and the back shelves of used bookstores, no promotion or social media posts). That's the kind of weird, small-scale work that actually excites me—work that doesn't scream for attention, just waits for the right person to find it.

No gallery, no tickets, no social media promotions. Just word-of-mouth whispers to people I think might sit with it.

The medium is foraged, found stuff: rotting logs split open to tuck tiny contact mics inside, rusted scrap metal strung like chimes that only hum when wind hits them at a specific angle, shed fox fur and crushed bone fragments tucked into clay indentations on the ground. The sound layer is half field recordings I capture on site—rain seeping through moss, termites chewing through beams, distant highway hum bleeding into the quiet—and half dissonant, layered vocal snippets: anonymous oral histories I collect from people who used to live or work in these spaces, talking about unspoken grief, missed chances, the way a place can vanish while you're still carrying it like a bruise.

It's interactive, but not in a playful way. If a visitor leans too close to a rotting log, the contact mic triggers a quiet clip of someone saying, "I still drive past here sometimes just to pretend it's still there." If they step on a patch of bare dirt where a house's foundation used to be, it plays a soft, static-laced story about a child who hid in the basement during storms, now grown up with no basement to hide in.

The style is messy, unpolished, deliberately unphotogenic. No clean lines, no curated "aesthetic." The materials are worn, used, broken. The sound never resolves into a melody; it hums and crackles and fades, like a half-remembered dream. It's temporary: I leave it up for two weeks max, then take every trace of it apart. I return the fur and bones to where I found them, bury the contact mics under a tree, smash the clay indentations with a rock. I keep a private journal with notes and a few blurry phone photos, but no one else gets documentation. No one gets to turn it into a reel or a print or a "viral moment."

The themes are the ones we don't like to name: the quiet violence of gentrification that erases not just buildings but memories, grief that has no funeral, the way we romanticize "wilderness" while ignoring the people who tended these spaces for generations, the small, uncelebrated acts of survival that leave no mark on the world. It's not supposed to comfort anyone. It's supposed to make you stand in the overgrown dirt and feel the weight of the place, the way it's still alive even when everyone has forgotten it.

I don't want to make art that sells. I don't want to make art that makes people feel good. I want to make art that demands you pay attention, even if it's uncomfortable, even if you leave feeling restless instead of inspired. That's the only kind of art that ever actually matters to me."}
